description: I love a challenge; it makes for a good learning experience.
summary: We tried to tackle the harmonization of data between the two classes of satellites, we got some insights from the data and the Jupyter notebooks, but more work is needed to converge them. We also made good progress on interfaces that work best for seeing historical data in aggregate: a useful companion to the live FIRMS tool. Namely, a 26-year Burning Activity Calendar for Canada, a Region view where raw and corrected data sit side by side, and a Timeline view (with some playful inspiration from Git). This is, hopefully, an alpha of a single pane of glass for all MODIS and VIIRS data, and we see in it a useful tool for scientists and fire managers.
details:
FireBAC is a 26-year burning activity record for Canada (other regions to come), built from NASA FIRMS MODIS and VIIRS active-fire detections: 40 country-year files, 632 MB, 8.25 million detections. Python does all of the science and publishes the results as artifacts, and the site is a static front end that only reads them.

The two sensors do not agree. Counted raw, VIIRS reports 3.21 times more detections than MODIS. Matching both to the same 0.01° cell on the same day brings that down to 2.08, and what is left is not a constant: it depends on how many VIIRS pixels the fire covers. A single pixel means MODIS sees it 14 % of the time, eight or more means 65 %. We fitted that as four bins, which corrects isolated detections by 7.34× and dense clusters by 1.55×, calibrated on 2012–2022 and applied unchanged to 2023–2025, so the most recent years are a test rather than a refit.

On top of that we built the interfaces we actually wanted for reading history. A calendar, where 26 years sit against 12 months and you can switch between counts and an anomaly score against the 2012–2022 median. A region view, where you draw an area and see raw MODIS, raw VIIRS and our estimate in separate columns, never summed, with the detections behind the search downloadable as CSV. And a timeline that shows every satellite pass over a place as a log, with some playful inspiration from Git. The point is to be a companion to the live FIRMS map: FIRMS tells you where the fire is now, this tells you what is normal for that place and whether the answer depends on which satellite was watching.

The intended impact is continuity. Suomi NPP stopped delivering on 2 November 2026, so the record has to continue on another platform without changing what it means. We tested the same curve on NOAA-20 and it matches Suomi NPP to within 0.007 across all four bins, on the same landscape. The shape transfers; the level is calibrated per region, which is why Argentina gets a different fit and why we say so instead of quoting one global number.

We used Python 3.12 with uv, DuckDB, pandas, NumPy and PyArrow for the data, and Vue 3, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind, ECharts, canvas maps, DuckDB-WASM and Apache Arrow for the site, with bun and Vitest around it. The creative part was mostly about choosing surfaces: the calendar as the hero rather than a wall of charts, the Git metaphor for passes, and the correction shown as a table beside the raw counts instead of being applied silently.

We also spent a lot of time deciding what not to claim. The matching unit moves the level, so a 3×3 neighbourhood takes 0.29 to 0.68, and changing the grid takes 16.6 % to 27.6 %, which is why the published number is a co-location indicator at 0.01° and not a detection probability. VIIRS FRP is censored at 367 K, confidence scales are not comparable between sensors, burned area was rejected because it records a day of burn and not sub-daily timing, and the unit is a cell-day, so we publish no fire-event count. 2000–2002 keep their counts but carry no anomaly score, because the archive is incomplete there and colouring it would have invented a drought which is way we opted for graying them out.
